analysis.one_liner: Triples cleanup penalties on companies that sold mercury- or PCB-contaminated sites to homebuyers and pays residents who lived there.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced: introduced with no cosponsors, it sat in two House subcommittees for the rest of the 106th Congress and never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the Superfund law, people who bought or lived on contaminated property generally had little direct way to recover from the company that polluted it. This bill would have required any company that disposed of mercury, PCBs, or similar toxins at a site and then sold or leased it when residential use was foreseeable to pay three times the cleanup costs and damages on top of what it already owed. The money could be recovered by the EPA or by anyone who lived at the property after the sale, and would be divided among those residents. Homebuyers and small developers who bought in good faith and did not cause the pollution would be exempt.
analysis.who_benefits: Families who bought or rented homes on land a polluter had contaminated and then sold off — including people displaced from those homes. They could sue for triple cleanup costs and damages, or receive a share of what the EPA recovers, without needing to prove fault through the normal defenses the polluter might otherwise raise.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Residents of contaminated former industrial sites

how_it_helps.text: It makes a polluter liable for three times the cleanup costs or damages it would otherwise owe under the Superfund law if it disposed of designated hazardous substances at a facility and then sold, leased, or conveyed it under circumstances where future residential use was reasonably foreseeable [S2][S3].

The recovery is available to the EPA or to any person who lives or previously lived at the property after it was sold, and any money recovered must be equitably allocated among those residents [S2][S3].

Liability applies without regard to the normal defenses to Superfund liability, and the amounts are in addition to existing recoveries, so residents are not squeezed out by defenses like the statute of limitations or contractor defenses [S2][S3].

Homebuyers who bought primarily as a personal residence, did not cause the contamination, and took due care are exempt, as are unaffiliated small businesses with fewer than 25 employees and under $2 million in annual revenue buying for residential development [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Companies that contaminated sites with mercury, PCBs, tetrachloroethylene, or similar toxins and then sold or leased those sites for homes — they would face triple damages on top of existing Superfund liability, plus defense costs if a suit was filed against a party the bill exempts.
analysis.who_pays_short: Industrial polluters who sold contaminated land

drawbacks.text: Triple damages on top of standard Superfund liability raises the cost of cleanup-related litigation sharply, and the bill applies only to a named list of substances (mercury, PCBs, tetrachloroethylenes) plus whatever else the EPA Administrator later designates, so liability lines would be drawn by regulation [S2][S3].

The bill protects small homebuyers and small residential developers, but a larger developer or landlord who bought a contaminated site for homes and took due care would still face treble exposure, which could discourage redevelopment of brownfield sites — the very cleanup the Superfund law tries to encourage [S3].
A person who sues a party that turns out to be exempt must pay that party's attorney and expert fees, so a family would need a strong case before filing or risk paying the defense's bills [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the narrow group of families who lived on contaminated land after it was sold, the bill offered a direct, enlarged remedy when existing Superfund law gave them little. The costs fall on polluters and, to a lesser extent, on larger residential developers of former industrial sites, and the small-business exemption plus fee-shifting limits the burden on genuinely innocent buyers. The design is narrow and targeted rather than sweeping, but its narrowness also means most contaminated residents would not be covered — it applies only where the site was already subject to a cleanup action and the residential use was foreseeable at the time of sale.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to two House committees, then to subcommittees, and sat there with no hearing, no vote, and no cosponsors until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Robert Menendez introduced the bill on April 14, 1999 [S1][S3].

It was referred to the Commerce Committee and the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee on the day of introduction, then on April 19 to the Water Resources and Environment Subcommittee and on May 5 to the Finance and Hazardous Materials Subcommittee [S5].
No further action was taken before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001, so the bill never reached the House floor [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that disposed of mercury, PCBs, or similar toxins and sold contaminated sites for homes kept the ordinary Superfund liability rules, with no treble-damages remedy and no direct payout channel for the residents who lived there.

for.name: Rep. Robert Menendez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to create a treble-damages remedy for residents of contaminated properties sold for residential use.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee (Finance and Hazardous Materials Subcommittee)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled, and it died there at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: With a single sponsor and zero cosponsors, no voting record exists to show how parties would have lined up.

industries.note: The bill would have tripled their liability where they contaminated a site and then sold it for foreseeable residential use. Their interest in the bill ran against the residents living on that land.

Small homebuyers and developers under 25 employees and $2 million in revenue would be exempt, but larger developers and landlords acquiring contaminated sites for homes would face treble exposure, which could discourage brownfield redevelopment.
